subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung anatomy: lobes, fissures, and foreign body aspiration
vignette: A 19-year-old man reviews chest radiograph anatomy. He notes that the right and left lungs are asymmetric: one side has three lobes separated by two fissures, while the other has only two lobes and a lingula. He wants to recall which lung normally has the greater number of lobes.
question: Which lung normally has three lobes?

options.text: Neither; each lung has two lobes
Only the left lung, when a cardiac notch is present

explanation_correct: The right lung has three lobes: upper, middle, and lower (RUL, RML, RLL), separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures. The left lung has only two lobes because the middle-lobe region is replaced by the cardiac notch, the space occupied by the heart. Instead of a middle lobe, the left lung has the lingula, which is the homolog of the right middle lobe. This asymmetry between the two lungs is a classic anatomic distinction.

explanation_incorrect.B: The left lung has only two lobes (upper and lower); it lacks a middle lobe and instead has the lingula and cardiac notch.
explanation_incorrect.C: The lungs are not equal: the right has three lobes and the left has two.
explanation_incorrect.D: The right lung has three lobes, so the claim that each lung has only two is false.
explanation_incorrect.E: It is the right lung that has three lobes; the left lung has two lobes plus the cardiac notch, not three.

educationalObjective: The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, lower); the left lung has two lobes plus a lingula and cardiac notch.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung anatomy: lobes, fissures, and foreign body aspiration
vignette: A 24-year-old woman reviews the differences between the right and left lungs during an anatomy session. She learns that the left lung lacks a middle lobe because of the cardiac notch but retains a small tongue-like projection near its anterior border. She wants to identify the embryologic counterpart of this projection.
question: The lingula of the left lung is the homolog of which structure?
explanation_correct: The left lung has fewer lobes (two) and a lingula; instead of a middle lobe, it has a space occupied by the heart (the cardiac notch). The lingula is the homolog of the right middle lobe. Just as the right middle lobe is separated from the right lower lobe by the horizontal fissure, the lingula represents the left-sided counterpart of that middle-lobe tissue. Recognizing this homolog helps explain why the left lung has only two lobes.

explanation_incorrect.A: The right upper lobe is not the homolog of the lingula; the lingula corresponds to middle-lobe tissue, not upper-lobe tissue.
explanation_incorrect.B: The right lower lobe is separated by the oblique fissure and is not the counterpart of the lingula.
explanation_incorrect.C: The left lower lobe is a separate lobe on the left; the lingula is a distinct structure and is not a homolog of the lower lobe.
explanation_incorrect.E: Although the lingula is adjacent to left upper lobe tissue, it is specifically the homolog of the right middle lobe, not of the left upper lobe itself.

educationalObjective: The lingula is the left lung's homolog of the right middle lobe, which is absent because the heart occupies that space.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung anatomy: lobes, fissures, and foreign body aspiration
vignette: A 30-year-old radiology resident reviews hilar anatomy on a chest CT before a bronchoscopy procedure. She recalls the mnemonic RALS, which describes the relationship of the pulmonary artery to the bronchus at each lung hilum. She needs to identify the correct relationship on the right side before documenting the findings.
question: At the right lung hilum, the pulmonary artery lies in which position relative to the bronchus?
explanation_correct: The relationship of the pulmonary artery to the bronchus at each hilum is described by the mnemonic RALS: Right Anterior, Left Superior. At the right hilum, the pulmonary artery lies anterior to the bronchus. At the left hilum, the pulmonary artery lies superior to the bronchus. Remembering this relationship helps orient structures on cross-sectional imaging and during hilar surgery.

explanation_incorrect.A: The artery is superior to the bronchus on the LEFT (the 'LS' of RALS), not on the right.
explanation_incorrect.C: Posterior is not correct; on the right the artery is anterior to the bronchus.
explanation_incorrect.D: Inferior is not the described relationship; RALS specifies anterior on the right and superior on the left.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lateral is not the relationship captured by RALS; the key right-sided relationship is anterior.

educationalObjective: RALS = Right Anterior, Left Superior describes the pulmonary artery's position relative to the bronchus at the hila.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung anatomy: lobes, fissures, and foreign body aspiration
vignette: A 52-year-old man with hemoptysis undergoes CT angiography of the chest. The radiologist identifies the carina, the ridge where the trachea divides into the mainstem bronchi, and notes its relationship to the great vessels before a mediastinal biopsy. The carina is described as lying posterior to one major vessel and anteromedial to another.
question: Which of the following correctly describes the position of the carina relative to the aorta?

options.text: Anterior to the ascending aorta and posterior to the descending aorta
Anterior to both the ascending and descending aorta
Posterior to the descending aorta and lateral to the ascending aorta
Inferior to the aortic arch with no consistent relationship to either vessel
Posterior to the ascending aorta and anteromedial to the descending aorta

explanation_correct: The carina is posterior to the ascending aorta and anteromedial to the descending aorta. This relationship is a useful landmark on cross-sectional imaging of the mediastinum. The trachea bifurcates at the level of the carina, which corresponds to T4 (recall the mnemonic that the trachea bifurcates at T4). Knowing the carina's relation to the great vessels helps localize mediastinal lesions and plan procedures.

explanation_incorrect.A: The carina is posterior (not anterior) to the ascending aorta; this option reverses the correct relationship.
explanation_incorrect.B: The carina is not anterior to both vessels; it is posterior to the ascending aorta and anteromedial to the descending aorta.
explanation_incorrect.C: The carina is anteromedial (not posterior) to the descending aorta and lies directly posterior, not lateral, to the ascending aorta.
explanation_incorrect.D: There is a consistent, testable relationship — posterior to the ascending aorta and anteromedial to the descending aorta — so 'no consistent relationship' is wrong.

educationalObjective: The carina lies posterior to the ascending aorta and anteromedial to the descending aorta.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung anatomy: lobes, fissures, and foreign body aspiration
vignette: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after suddenly choking while eating peanuts. He has acute dyspnea, wheezing, and decreased breath sounds over the right lung. Bronchoscopy confirms an aspirated peanut lodged in a mainstem bronchus. The physician notes that foreign bodies preferentially enter one mainstem bronchus because of its anatomic orientation.
question: Which feature of the right mainstem bronchus best explains why inhaled foreign bodies more commonly lodge there?

options.text: It is longer and narrower than the left mainstem bronchus
It is lined by pseudostratified epithelium that traps particles
It is wider, more vertical, and shorter than the left mainstem bronchus
It contains more cartilage rings than the left mainstem bronchus
It arises at a sharper angle from the trachea than the left mainstem bronchus

explanation_correct: The right mainstem bronchus is wider, more vertical, and shorter than the left, so inhaled objects more easily pass into it. This is why aspirated foreign bodies are more common on the right side. In contrast, the left mainstem bronchus is longer, narrower, and more horizontal, making it a less direct pathway. The anatomic orientation, not epithelial lining or cartilage content, is the determining factor.

explanation_incorrect.A: The right mainstem bronchus is shorter and wider, not longer and narrower; the left is the longer, narrower one.
explanation_incorrect.B: Both mainstem bronchi are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; the difference in aspiration risk is due to geometry, not epithelial lining.
explanation_incorrect.D: The number of cartilage rings is not the reason; the relevant feature is that the right bronchus is wider, more vertical, and shorter.
explanation_incorrect.E: The right bronchus is more vertical, a more direct continuation of the trachea, rather than arising at a sharper angle; the left arises at the sharper angle.

educationalObjective: The right mainstem bronchus is wider, more vertical, and shorter, predisposing to right-sided foreign body aspiration.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung anatomy: lobes, fissures, and foreign body aspiration
vignette: A 68-year-old man who is bedridden accidentally aspirates a small piece of food while lying flat on his back. He develops a cough and localized crackles, and a chest radiograph shows a density in the dependent portion of the right lung. The treating physician recalls that the segment into which an aspirated object travels depends on the patient's position at the time of aspiration.
question: In a supine patient, an inhaled foreign body most commonly enters which location?

options.text: Superior segment of the right lower lobe or posterior segment of the right upper lobe
Anterior segment of the right upper lobe
Apical segment of the left upper lobe

explanation_correct: When a person aspirates while supine, the foreign body usually enters the superior segment of the right lower lobe, or sometimes the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. These are the most dependent (posterior) segments when the patient is lying on the back. Because the right mainstem bronchus is wider, more vertical, and shorter, the right lung is the more common side. This is why aspiration in supine patients often involves the posterior upper-lobe or superior lower-lobe segments.

explanation_incorrect.B: The anterior segment of the right upper lobe is not the classic dependent segment in a supine patient; the posterior segment of the RUL is favored instead.
explanation_incorrect.C: The right middle lobe is not the typical destination in a supine aspirator; the superior segment of the RLL or posterior segment of the RUL is more common.
explanation_incorrect.D: The left lower lobe is possible but much less common because the right mainstem bronchus is the more direct pathway; supine aspiration favors the right side.
explanation_incorrect.E: The apical segment of the left upper lobe is not a classic site for supine aspiration; both the side (left) and segment (apical) are atypical.

educationalObjective: In a supine patient, aspirated material typically enters the superior segment of the right lower lobe or the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung anatomy: lobes, fissures, and foreign body aspiration
vignette: A 35-year-old man is walking upright when he suddenly aspirates a small object while talking on the phone. He develops immediate coughing and localized wheezing. Bronchoscopy is planned, and the physician predicts the most likely location of the object based on the patient's upright posture at the time of aspiration.
question: In an upright (standing) patient, an inhaled foreign body most commonly enters which location?

options.text: Posterior segment of the right upper lobe
Superior segment of the right lower lobe

explanation_correct: When aspiration occurs while upright, the inhaled object most commonly enters the right lower lobe, because gravity directs it down the more vertical right mainstem bronchus into the lower lobe. This contrasts with the supine position, where the superior segment of the right lower lobe or posterior segment of the right upper lobe is favored, and with lying on the right side or prone, where the right upper lobe is the usual site. Position at the time of aspiration is therefore a key determinant of where the object lodges.

explanation_incorrect.A: The posterior segment of the right upper lobe is typical of supine aspiration, not upright aspiration.
explanation_incorrect.B: The superior segment of the right lower lobe is the classic site in a supine patient; upright aspiration more commonly enters the right lower lobe as a whole.
explanation_incorrect.C: The right middle lobe is not the most common destination for an upright aspirator; gravity favors the lower lobe.
explanation_incorrect.E: The left upper lobe is an unlikely site; the right mainstem bronchus is the more direct and wider pathway, and gravity favors the lower lobes when upright.

educationalObjective: Upright aspiration most often sends a foreign body into the right lower lobe, whereas supine aspiration favors the superior RLL or posterior RUL, and prone or right-side-lying favors the RUL.
